questions.prompt: Which statement best describes General Science as a Grade 10 learning area?
options: An integrated study of biology, chemistry, and physics ideas
A subject that only studies business records
A study of historical events and citizenship
A language course focused on grammar rules
questions.correctAnswer: An integrated study of biology, chemistry, and physics ideas
questions.explanation: General Science brings together ideas from biology, chemistry, and physics to explain natural events and solve practical problems.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the meaning of General Science as a learning area.

questions.prompt: Which set lists the main branches commonly studied in General Science?
options: Biology, Chemistry, and Physics
History, Geography, and Civics
Music, Drama, and Dance
Accounting, Marketing, and Banking
questions.correctAnswer: Biology, Chemistry, and Physics
questions.explanation: General Science uses the core science branches of Biology, Chemistry, and Physics to study living things, matter, energy, and forces.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify the main branches of General Science.

questions.prompt: A learner observes that bean seedlings placed near a window bend toward the light. What is the best scientific inference?
options: Light affects the direction of shoot growth
Bean plants grow only in glass containers
Windows add minerals to seedlings
Soil stops plants from responding to light
questions.correctAnswer: Light affects the direction of shoot growth
questions.explanation: An inference is a logical conclusion drawn from observations and evidence. The bending seedlings suggest a response to light.
questions.learningOutcome: Use evidence from observations to draw simple scientific inferences.

questions.prompt: A school wants to know whether a nearby stream is safe for irrigation. Which information would give the strongest scientific evidence?
options: Results from testing pH, turbidity, and dissolved chemicals
The colour of a poster about the stream
The number of learners who like the stream
A rumour that the stream was clean last year
questions.correctAnswer: Results from testing pH, turbidity, and dissolved chemicals
questions.explanation: Scientific conclusions should be based on measurable evidence. Water tests provide data that can be checked and compared.
questions.learningOutcome: Select appropriate evidence for drawing conclusions in science.

questions.prompt: Which investigation plan best tests whether fertiliser affects maize seedling height?
options: Grow equal groups of maize with and without fertiliser while keeping water, soil, and light the same
Grow one maize seed in shade and another bean seed in sunlight
Ask learners which maize plants look healthier without measuring them
Change fertiliser, water, seed type, and soil for every plant
questions.correctAnswer: Grow equal groups of maize with and without fertiliser while keeping water, soil, and light the same
questions.explanation: A fair test changes only the factor being investigated. Keeping other conditions constant makes the conclusion more reliable.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse a simple investigation design for fair collection of evidence.

questions.prompt: Which cell structure controls most activities of a plant or animal cell?
options: Nucleus
Cell wall
Vacuole
Ribosome
questions.correctAnswer: Nucleus
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains genetic material and controls many cell activities such as growth and reproduction.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify cell structures and state their functions.

questions.prompt: Why can an electron microscope show more detail than a light microscope?
options: It has much higher resolving power
It uses larger glass slides
It does not need a specimen
It makes living cells grow faster
questions.correctAnswer: It has much higher resolving power
questions.explanation: Electron microscopes use beams of electrons, giving higher resolution and allowing smaller structures to be seen clearly.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain differences between light and electron microscopes.

questions.prompt: Which pair of structures is usually found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
options: Cell wall and chloroplasts
Nucleus and cytoplasm
Mitochondria and ribosomes
Cell membrane and nucleus
questions.correctAnswer: Cell wall and chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Plant cells commonly have a cellulose cell wall and chloroplasts for photosynthesis. Animal cells do not have these structures.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare plant and animal cell structures.

questions.prompt: Which sequence shows the correct order of biological organisation from simplest to most complex?
options: Organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
Organism, organ system, organ, tissue, cell, organelle
Cell, organelle, tissue, organ, organism, organ system
Tissue, cell, organelle, organism, organ, organ system
questions.correctAnswer: Organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
questions.explanation: Living things are organised from small cell parts to cells, tissues, organs, systems, and the whole organism.
questions.learningOutcome: Construct a concept map of levels of cell organisation.

questions.prompt: A cell that needs a lot of energy, such as a muscle cell, is likely to contain many of which organelle?
options: Mitochondria
Cell walls
Large central vacuoles
Chloroplasts
questions.correctAnswer: Mitochondria
questions.explanation: Mitochondria release energy during aerobic respiration, so active cells often have many mitochondria.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate cell organelles to their functions in living organisms.

questions.prompt: A learner sees ribosomes, mitochondria, a cell membrane, and no chloroplasts in a micrograph. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
options: The specimen could be an animal cell
The specimen must be a xylem vessel
The specimen is a virus
The specimen is a starch grain
questions.correctAnswer: The specimen could be an animal cell
questions.explanation: Animal cells have a cell membrane, mitochondria, and ribosomes, but they do not have chloroplasts.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse cell features to distinguish plant and animal cells.

questions.prompt: Which model would best help younger learners understand that cells form tissues and tissues form organs?
options: A labelled nested chart moving from cells to tissues to organs
A list of unrelated scientific careers
A map showing counties in Kenya
A table of only chemical symbols
questions.correctAnswer: A labelled nested chart moving from cells to tissues to organs
questions.explanation: A nested chart shows how smaller biological units combine to make larger structures in an organism.
questions.learningOutcome: Create a representation of levels of organisation in organisms.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme begins the digestion of starch in the mouth?
options: Salivary amylase
Pepsin
Lipase
Trypsin
questions.correctAnswer: Salivary amylase
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase starts breaking starch into smaller sugars in the mouth.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe digestion of different food types in the digestive system.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of bile in fat digestion?
options: It emulsifies fats into tiny droplets
It converts proteins into amino acids
It changes starch into glucose
It absorbs water from undigested food
questions.correctAnswer: It emulsifies fats into tiny droplets
questions.explanation: Bile breaks large fat droplets into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase action.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain digestion of fats in the human digestive system.

questions.prompt: Which adaptation makes the small intestine efficient at absorbing digested food?
options: Many villi with thin walls and rich blood supply
A thick enamel coating
A hard outer seed coat
Large air sacs for breathing
questions.correctAnswer: Many villi with thin walls and rich blood supply
questions.explanation: Villi increase surface area and have thin walls plus blood vessels for quick absorption and transport of nutrients.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain adaptations of parts of the human digestive system.

questions.prompt: A food sample turns violet when mixed with Biuret reagent. Which nutrient is present?
options: Protein
Starch
Reducing sugar
Fat
questions.correctAnswer: Protein
questions.explanation: Biuret reagent changes from blue to violet when protein is present.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret results from food tests for nutrients.

questions.prompt: Why does the oesophagus have circular and longitudinal muscles?
options: To push food by peristalsis toward the stomach
To produce bile for fat digestion
To absorb most amino acids
To grind food using enamel
questions.correctAnswer: To push food by peristalsis toward the stomach
questions.explanation: Alternating contraction and relaxation of muscles in the oesophagus moves food along by peristalsis.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse adaptations of digestive organs to their functions.

questions.prompt: Which procedure best distinguishes a food containing both starch and protein from one containing only starch?
options: Use iodine solution and Biuret reagent on separate portions of each food
Heat both foods until they burn and compare smoke colour only
Add water to both foods and check which one floats
Smell both foods and record the stronger smell
questions.correctAnswer: Use iodine solution and Biuret reagent on separate portions of each food
questions.explanation: Iodine tests for starch while Biuret reagent tests for protein. Testing separate portions avoids mixing reagents.
questions.learningOutcome: Plan suitable food tests to identify nutrients in samples.

questions.prompt: Which plant tissue mainly transports water and mineral salts from roots to leaves?
options: Xylem
Phloem
Epidermis
Cambium
questions.correctAnswer: Xylem
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and mineral salts upward through the plant and also helps support the stem.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify transport tissues in plants and their roles.

questions.prompt: What is translocation in flowering plants?
options: Movement of manufactured food through phloem
Loss of water vapour from leaves
Absorption of oxygen by root hairs
Splitting of water during photosynthesis
questions.correctAnswer: Movement of manufactured food through phloem
questions.explanation: Translocation is the movement of sugars and other manufactured food substances through the phloem.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe transport of manufactured food in plants.

questions.prompt: How are root hair cells adapted for absorbing water and mineral salts?
options: They have a long projection that gives a large surface area
They contain thick waxy cuticle to stop all water movement
They have no cell membrane
They are filled with air spaces only
questions.correctAnswer: They have a long projection that gives a large surface area
questions.explanation: Root hairs increase the surface area in contact with soil water, helping absorption of water and dissolved minerals.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain absorption of water and mineral salts by root hairs.

questions.prompt: On a windy afternoon, a bean plant loses water faster than on a calm morning. Which process has increased?
options: Transpiration
Fertilisation
Pollination
Germination
questions.correctAnswer: Transpiration
questions.explanation: Wind removes moist air around leaves, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient for water vapour loss.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate environmental factors to the rate of transpiration.

questions.prompt: Which comparison between xylem and phloem is most accurate?
options: Xylem vessels are mostly dead and transport water; phloem sieve tubes are living and transport food
Xylem transports hormones only; phloem transports oxygen only
Xylem is found only in roots; phloem is found only in leaves
Xylem and phloem both transport only undigested starch
questions.correctAnswer: Xylem vessels are mostly dead and transport water; phloem sieve tubes are living and transport food
questions.explanation: Xylem and phloem are both vascular tissues, but they differ in structure and the substances they transport.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare plant transport tissues and their functions.

questions.prompt: Which setup best investigates the effect of leaf surface area on transpiration?
options: Use similar shoots in potometers, reduce leaves on one shoot, and keep light, wind, and temperature constant
Use one dry stick and one flowering plant in different rooms
Measure only the height of two plants growing in different soils
Put leaves in sugar solution and record their colour after a week
questions.correctAnswer: Use similar shoots in potometers, reduce leaves on one shoot, and keep light, wind, and temperature constant
questions.explanation: A controlled potometer investigation can compare water uptake when leaf area changes while other conditions remain the same.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a fair investigation on factors affecting transpiration.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of respiration in living cells?
options: To release energy from food
To make soil particles larger
To produce glass from sand
To change water into mineral salts
questions.correctAnswer: To release energy from food
questions.explanation: Respiration breaks down food substances such as glucose to release energy needed for cell activities.
questions.learningOutcome: State the purpose of respiration in living organisms.

questions.prompt: Which word equation represents aerobic respiration?
options: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy
Carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen
Nitrogen + oxygen -> ammonia + energy
Protein + iodine -> starch + water
questions.correctAnswer: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose, producing carbon dioxide, water, and energy.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe aerobic respiration using a word equation.

questions.prompt: When a person breathes out through limewater, the limewater turns milky. What does this show?
options: Exhaled air contains carbon dioxide
Exhaled air contains no water vapour
Inhaled air is pure oxygen
Limewater detects nitrogen gas
questions.correctAnswer: Exhaled air contains carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to form a milky calcium carbonate suspension.
questions.learningOutcome: Use tests to identify products of respiration.

questions.prompt: Which products are formed when yeast respires anaerobically in a sugar solution?
options: Ethanol and carbon dioxide
Oxygen and starch
Water and nitrogen
Protein and bile
questions.correctAnswer: Ethanol and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Yeast fermentation breaks down sugar without oxygen to form ethanol, carbon dioxide, and some energy.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe anaerobic respiration in yeast and its products.

questions.prompt: After sprinting, a learner breathes faster for several minutes. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: Extra oxygen is needed to oxidise lactic acid formed during anaerobic respiration
The lungs are digesting starch from the meal
The heart has stopped pumping blood to muscles
The muscles are producing chlorophyll
questions.correctAnswer: Extra oxygen is needed to oxidise lactic acid formed during anaerobic respiration
questions.explanation: Vigorous exercise can cause oxygen debt. Faster breathing supplies oxygen to break down accumulated lactic acid.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse the relationship between exercise, anaerobic respiration, and oxygen debt.

questions.prompt: Which plan best investigates how temperature affects the rate of respiration in yeast?
options: Place equal yeast-sugar mixtures at different temperatures and measure carbon dioxide produced in equal time
Use different amounts of sugar, yeast, and water at random temperatures
Observe dry yeast grains without adding sugar solution
Compare maize seeds and yeast in different containers with no measurements
questions.correctAnswer: Place equal yeast-sugar mixtures at different temperatures and measure carbon dioxide produced in equal time
questions.explanation: The plan changes temperature only and measures carbon dioxide production, a useful indicator of yeast respiration rate.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a fair test on factors affecting respiration rate.

questions.prompt: What is germination?
options: The process by which a seed develops into a seedling
The transfer of pollen to a stigma
The movement of sugar in phloem
The drying of leaves after harvest
questions.correctAnswer: The process by which a seed develops into a seedling
questions.explanation: Germination begins when a viable seed resumes growth and the embryo develops into a seedling.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the concept of germination as part of plant growth.

questions.prompt: Which conditions are generally necessary for most seeds to germinate?
options: Water, oxygen, and suitable temperature
Bright light, salt water, and no air
Dry soil, oil, and darkness only
Carbon monoxide, fertiliser, and no water
questions.correctAnswer: Water, oxygen, and suitable temperature
questions.explanation: Most seeds need water to activate enzymes, oxygen for respiration, and a suitable temperature for metabolic reactions.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify conditions necessary for seed germination.

questions.prompt: Why is seed dormancy useful to a plant species?
options: It delays germination until conditions are favourable
It stops seeds from ever growing
It turns roots into flowers
It prevents all respiration in mature plants
questions.correctAnswer: It delays germination until conditions are favourable
questions.explanation: Dormancy helps seeds survive unfavourable conditions and germinate when water, temperature, or other conditions improve.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the importance of seed dormancy in plant survival.

questions.prompt: A shoot bends toward light from a window. Which explanation best describes this phototropic response?
options: Auxin causes cells on the shaded side to elongate more
Water evaporates faster on the lit side and pulls the shoot
Chlorophyll moves from roots to the window
The root pushes the shoot toward the glass
questions.correctAnswer: Auxin causes cells on the shaded side to elongate more
questions.explanation: In shoots, auxin builds up on the shaded side and promotes cell elongation, causing bending toward light.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate plant hormones to growth responses.

questions.prompt: Which observation best shows the difference between plant growth and plant development?
options: A stem becomes longer while flower buds also form
A dry seed remains unchanged in a packet
A leaf is cut into equal pieces
A plant label is moved from one pot to another
questions.correctAnswer: A stem becomes longer while flower buds also form
questions.explanation: Growth involves increase in size, while development involves changes in form and function such as formation of flowers.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse differences between growth and development in plants.

questions.prompt: Which method would best help germinate seeds with very hard seed coats during a school investigation?
options: Gently scarify the seed coat before soaking
Boil the seeds until the embryos are destroyed
Store the seeds in a dry tin without air
Paint the seeds with oil to block water entry
questions.correctAnswer: Gently scarify the seed coat before soaking
questions.explanation: Scarification weakens a hard seed coat, allowing water and oxygen to reach the embryo without killing it.
questions.learningOutcome: Select a suitable method for breaking seed dormancy in practical work.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes microorganisms?
options: Living things too small to be seen clearly without magnification
Large animals that always live in forests
Only non-living particles found in air
Plants with large visible flowers
questions.correctAnswer: Living things too small to be seen clearly without magnification
questions.explanation: Microorganisms include tiny organisms such as bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and some algae that usually require a microscope.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe microorganisms and give examples.

questions.prompt: Which useful role can bacteria play in agriculture?
options: Fixing nitrogen in legume root nodules
Changing copper into plastic
Stopping all decomposition in soil
Making leaves unable to photosynthesise
questions.correctAnswer: Fixing nitrogen in legume root nodules
questions.explanation: Some bacteria in legume root nodules convert nitrogen into forms plants can use, improving soil fertility.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain useful roles of microorganisms in the environment.

questions.prompt: Why is pasteurisation used when processing milk?
options: To reduce harmful microorganisms while keeping milk usable
To turn all milk sugar into starch
To remove all calcium from milk
To make milk unable to mix with water
questions.correctAnswer: To reduce harmful microorganisms while keeping milk usable
questions.explanation: Pasteurisation heats milk for a controlled time to reduce disease-causing microorganisms and improve safety.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate control of microorganisms to food safety.

questions.prompt: A compost heap becomes warm and slowly changes plant waste into dark humus. Which organisms are mainly responsible?
options: Decomposing bacteria and fungi
Adult mosquitoes only
Earth's magnetic field lines
Crystals of common salt
questions.correctAnswer: Decomposing bacteria and fungi
questions.explanation: Bacteria and fungi break down dead organic matter, releasing heat and forming humus during decomposition.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply knowledge of microorganisms to decomposition and nutrient cycling.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes viruses different from bacteria?
options: Viruses reproduce only inside living host cells
Viruses have many chloroplasts
Viruses are larger than all animal cells
Viruses carry out photosynthesis in soil
questions.correctAnswer: Viruses reproduce only inside living host cells
questions.explanation: Viruses lack full cellular machinery and can multiply only after entering living host cells.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare major groups of microorganisms.

questions.prompt: During culture work, why should a Petri dish be opened for the shortest possible time?
options: To reduce contamination by unwanted microorganisms from air
To make agar change into glass
To stop all oxygen from entering forever
To increase the mass of the lid
questions.correctAnswer: To reduce contamination by unwanted microorganisms from air
questions.explanation: Aseptic technique limits entry of unwanted microorganisms, making observations safer and more reliable.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse safe techniques for handling microorganisms.

questions.prompt: Which plan best tests whether handwashing reduces microorganisms on learners' hands?
options: Press unwashed and washed fingertips on separate sterile agar plates, incubate safely, and compare colony numbers
Ask learners whether their hands look clean and record opinions only
Put soil on both hands and count grains of sand
Use one agar plate touched by many learners at different times without labels
questions.correctAnswer: Press unwashed and washed fingertips on separate sterile agar plates, incubate safely, and compare colony numbers
questions.explanation: The plan compares labelled samples before and after washing while measuring colony growth under controlled safety conditions.
questions.learningOutcome: Design a safe investigation on controlling microorganisms.

questions.prompt: What is the modern periodic table mainly arranged by?
options: Increasing atomic number
Increasing alphabetical order of element names
Increasing colour of elements
Increasing boiling point only
questions.correctAnswer: Increasing atomic number
questions.explanation: The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number, which is the number of protons.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe how elements are arranged in the periodic table.

questions.prompt: In the periodic table, what is a group?
options: A vertical column of elements
A horizontal row of elements
A single chemical equation
A mixture of compounds in water
questions.correctAnswer: A vertical column of elements
questions.explanation: A group is a vertical column. Elements in the same group often have similar chemical properties.
questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish between groups and periods in the periodic table.

questions.prompt: For many main-group elements, what does the group number show?
options: The number of electrons in the outer energy level
The number of neutrons in every isotope
The mass of one atom in kilograms
The number of compounds the element must form
questions.correctAnswer: The number of electrons in the outer energy level
questions.explanation: For many main-group elements, the group number relates to valence electrons, which influence bonding and reactivity.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate group position to valence electrons for main-group elements.

questions.prompt: Magnesium has atomic number 12 and electron arrangement 2,8,2. Where is it placed in the periodic table?
options: Group 2, Period 3
Group 3, Period 2
Group 8, Period 2
Group 12, Period 1
questions.correctAnswer: Group 2, Period 3
questions.explanation: Magnesium has two outer electrons, placing it in Group 2, and three occupied energy levels, placing it in Period 3.
questions.learningOutcome: Use electron arrangement to predict group and period.

questions.prompt: Why does atomic radius generally decrease from left to right across Period 3?
options: Nuclear charge increases while shielding changes little, pulling electrons closer
Atoms lose all their protons across the period
The number of occupied shells increases each step
All elements become noble gases immediately
questions.correctAnswer: Nuclear charge increases while shielding changes little, pulling electrons closer
questions.explanation: Across a period, increasing proton number attracts the same outer shell more strongly, so atomic radius tends to decrease.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain a trend in atomic size across a period.

questions.prompt: Element X has electron arrangement 2,8,7. Which prediction is most reasonable?
options: It is a Group 17 element that tends to gain one electron
It is a Group 1 metal that loses seven electrons
It is a noble gas with a complete outer shell
It is in Period 7 because it has seven outer electrons
questions.correctAnswer: It is a Group 17 element that tends to gain one electron
questions.explanation: An atom with seven valence electrons is a halogen-like Group 17 element and can gain one electron to complete its outer shell.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse electron arrangement to infer periodic table position and reactivity.

questions.prompt: A learner is given elements with atomic numbers 3, 11, and 19. Which classification best groups them?
options: They are Group 1 elements with one outer electron
They are Period 1 elements with full outer shells
They are Group 18 elements with no reactivity
They are non-metals with seven outer electrons
questions.correctAnswer: They are Group 1 elements with one outer electron
questions.explanation: Lithium, sodium, and potassium have one valence electron, so they belong to Group 1 and show related chemical behaviour.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify elements into periodic table groups using atomic number patterns.

questions.prompt: Which chemical family contains lithium, sodium, and potassium?
options: Alkali metals
Halogens
Noble gases
Transition metals
questions.correctAnswer: Alkali metals
questions.explanation: Lithium, sodium, and potassium are Group 1 elements known as alkali metals.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify common chemical families in the periodic table.

questions.prompt: Why are Group 17 elements called halogens?
options: They form salts when they react with metals
They are all unreactive gases
They all have two outer electrons
They are used only to make fertiliser
questions.correctAnswer: They form salts when they react with metals
questions.explanation: Halogen means salt-former. Halogens such as chlorine react with metals to form salts like chlorides.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe properties of halogens as a chemical family.

questions.prompt: Which property explains why noble gases are generally unreactive?
options: They have full outer electron shells
They have no protons in their nuclei
They always dissolve in acids
They are all solid at room temperature
questions.correctAnswer: They have full outer electron shells
questions.explanation: A full outer shell makes noble gas atoms stable, so they rarely gain, lose, or share electrons.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate electron arrangement to the reactivity of noble gases.

questions.prompt: Why does sodium react more vigorously with water than lithium?
options: Sodium's outer electron is farther from the nucleus and is lost more easily
Sodium has fewer electron shells than lithium
Lithium is a noble gas
Lithium has no outer electron
questions.correctAnswer: Sodium's outer electron is farther from the nucleus and is lost more easily
questions.explanation: Down Group 1, atoms have more shells, so the outer electron is less strongly attracted and is lost more easily.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain reactivity trends in alkali metals.

questions.prompt: Chlorine is bubbled into potassium bromide solution and the solution turns orange-brown. What does this show?
options: Chlorine displaces bromine because chlorine is more reactive
Bromine displaces chlorine because bromine is more reactive
Potassium becomes a noble gas
No reaction has occurred
questions.correctAnswer: Chlorine displaces bromine because chlorine is more reactive
questions.explanation: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its salt solution. Chlorine is more reactive than bromine.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse displacement reactions among halogens.

questions.prompt: An unknown family of elements forms ions with a 2+ charge and reacts with water less vigorously than Group 1 metals. Which family is most likely?
options: Alkaline earth metals
Halogens
Noble gases
Group 1 alkali metals
questions.correctAnswer: Alkaline earth metals
questions.explanation: Group 2 alkaline earth metals usually form 2+ ions and are generally less reactive with water than Group 1 metals.
questions.learningOutcome: Classify a chemical family from its reactivity and ion formation patterns.

questions.prompt: What is an ionic bond?
options: A strong attraction between oppositely charged ions
A force between neutral atoms that never exchange electrons
A bond formed only by sharing protons
A weak attraction between two wooden blocks
questions.correctAnswer: A strong attraction between oppositely charged ions
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding forms when electrons are transferred and the resulting positive and negative ions attract each other.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe ionic bonding in terms of electron transfer and ion attraction.

questions.prompt: What is a covalent bond?
options: A bond formed when atoms share electrons
A bond formed by dissolving salt in water
A bond between two magnets only
A bond formed when atoms lose all protons
questions.correctAnswer: A bond formed when atoms share electrons
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons to achieve more stable outer shells.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe covalent bonding in terms of shared electrons.

questions.prompt: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Which ions are formed?
options: Mg2+ and O2-
Mg2- and O2+
Mg+ and O-
Neutral Mg and neutral O only
questions.correctAnswer: Mg2+ and O2-
questions.explanation: Magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg2+, while oxygen gains two electrons to form O2-.
questions.learningOutcome: Predict ions formed during ionic bonding.

questions.prompt: Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity while solid sodium chloride does not?
options: Ions are free to move in the molten state but fixed in the solid lattice
Electrons disappear when salt melts
Solid sodium chloride contains no ions
Molten sodium chloride becomes a metal
questions.correctAnswer: Ions are free to move in the molten state but fixed in the solid lattice
questions.explanation: Electrical conduction in ionic substances requires mobile ions. In a solid lattice, the ions cannot move freely.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate ionic structure to electrical conductivity.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains the high melting point of sodium chloride?
options: Strong electrostatic attractions hold many oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice
Each sodium chloride molecule is held by a single weak bond only
The ions are separated by air spaces
Sodium chloride melts easily because it has no charged particles
questions.correctAnswer: Strong electrostatic attractions hold many oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice
questions.explanation: A lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong attractions throughout an ionic lattice.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain properties of ionic compounds using bonding and structure.

questions.prompt: Which bonding description fits water, H2O?
options: Oxygen shares electrons with two hydrogen atoms
Oxygen transfers two protons to hydrogen atoms
Hydrogen atoms become metal ions in a lattice
Water contains only free electrons and no atoms
questions.correctAnswer: Oxygen shares electrons with two hydrogen atoms
questions.explanation: Water is a covalent molecule in which oxygen shares electron pairs with hydrogen atoms.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse bonding in simple covalent molecules.

questions.prompt: Which model best represents bonding in calcium chloride, CaCl2?
options: One calcium atom loses two electrons, one to each of two chlorine atoms
Two calcium atoms each gain an electron from one chlorine atom
Calcium and chlorine share all electrons equally in a single molecule
Calcium becomes a noble gas by losing its nucleus
questions.correctAnswer: One calcium atom loses two electrons, one to each of two chlorine atoms
questions.explanation: Calcium forms Ca2+ by losing two electrons, and each chlorine gains one electron to form two Cl- ions.
questions.learningOutcome: Construct a particle model for ionic bonding in binary compounds.

questions.prompt: What colour change occurs when blue litmus paper is placed in an acid?
options: Blue to red
Red to blue
Blue to green
Red to colourless
questions.correctAnswer: Blue to red
questions.explanation: Acids turn blue litmus paper red, while bases turn red litmus paper blue.
questions.learningOutcome: Use indicators to identify acids and bases.

questions.prompt: A solution has pH 12. Which statement describes it correctly?
options: It is strongly alkaline
It is strongly acidic
It is exactly neutral
It must be pure water
questions.correctAnswer: It is strongly alkaline
questions.explanation: pH values above 7 indicate alkaline solutions, and values near 14 show strong alkalinity.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret pH values for acids, bases, and neutral solutions.

questions.prompt: What are the usual products of a reaction between an acid and a base?
options: Salt and water
Hydrogen and oxygen
Sugar and starch
Carbon and nitrogen
questions.correctAnswer: Salt and water
questions.explanation: Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base to form a salt and water.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe neutralisation reactions between acids and bases.

questions.prompt: Which solution is more acidic, one with pH 2 or one with pH 6?
options: The solution with pH 2
The solution with pH 6
Both are equally acidic
Neither is acidic because both are below 7
questions.correctAnswer: The solution with pH 2
questions.explanation: Lower pH values show stronger acidity. A solution at pH 2 is more acidic than one at pH 6.
questions.learningOutcome: Compare acidity using the pH scale.

questions.prompt: A piece of zinc is added to dilute hydrochloric acid and bubbles are produced. Which gas is formed?
options: Hydrogen
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Chlorine
questions.correctAnswer: Hydrogen
questions.explanation: Reactive metals such as zinc react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas.
questions.learningOutcome: Predict products when dilute acids react with metals.

questions.prompt: Which salt is formed when dilute sulfuric acid is completely neutralised by sodium hydroxide?
options: Sodium sulfate
Sodium chloride
Copper sulfate
Calcium carbonate
questions.correctAnswer: Sodium sulfate
questions.explanation: The sulfate ion from sulfuric acid combines with sodium ions from sodium hydroxide to form sodium sulfate.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse acid-base reactions to name salts formed.

questions.prompt: Which method best prepares pure dry copper(II) sulfate crystals from dilute sulfuric acid?
options: Add excess copper(II) oxide, warm gently, filter, then evaporate the filtrate to crystallisation point
Add excess sodium chloride, filter off the water, then burn the residue
Mix sulfuric acid with sand and dry the mixture directly
Add copper metal to cold acid and immediately collect crystals
questions.correctAnswer: Add excess copper(II) oxide, warm gently, filter, then evaporate the filtrate to crystallisation point
questions.explanation: An insoluble base can neutralise the acid. Excess solid is filtered off, and the salt solution is concentrated to form crystals.
questions.learningOutcome: Plan a safe preparation of a soluble salt from an acid and insoluble base.

questions.prompt: What is meant by the rate of a chemical reaction?
options: Change in amount of reactant or product per unit time
The total mass of glassware used
The colour of the laboratory bench
The number of elements in the periodic table
questions.correctAnswer: Change in amount of reactant or product per unit time
questions.explanation: Reaction rate describes how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed.
questions.learningOutcome: Define rate of reaction.

questions.prompt: Why does increasing temperature usually increase the rate of a reaction?
options: Particles move faster and collide more often with enough energy
Particles stop moving and settle at the bottom
Reactants become noble gases
The number of protons in every atom becomes zero
questions.correctAnswer: Particles move faster and collide more often with enough energy
questions.explanation: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, leading to more frequent successful collisions.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain the effect of temperature on reaction rate.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a catalyst in a chemical reaction?
options: It increases reaction rate without being used up
It always changes into the only product
It stops all particle collisions
It changes every acid into a metal
questions.correctAnswer: It increases reaction rate without being used up
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and remains chemically unchanged overall.
questions.learningOutcome: Describe how catalysts affect reaction rates.

questions.prompt: Powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with dilute hydrochloric acid than marble chips of the same mass. Why?
options: Powder has a larger surface area exposed to acid
Powder contains no calcium carbonate
Marble chips are already neutralised
Powder has fewer particles touching acid
questions.correctAnswer: Powder has a larger surface area exposed to acid
questions.explanation: Smaller particles expose more surface area, allowing more frequent collisions between acid particles and calcium carbonate.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply the effect of surface area on reaction rate.

questions.prompt: A learner doubles the concentration of acid reacting with magnesium ribbon. What is the likely effect on the initial reaction rate?
options: It increases because acid particles collide with magnesium more often
It becomes zero because concentration stops collisions
It decreases because magnesium turns into a noble gas
It stays exactly the same in all reactions
questions.correctAnswer: It increases because acid particles collide with magnesium more often
questions.explanation: Higher concentration means more reacting particles per unit volume, so successful collisions occur more frequently.
questions.learningOutcome: Relate concentration to collision frequency in reactions.

questions.prompt: Which pair of experiments fairly tests the effect of concentration on reaction rate?
options: Same magnesium length and temperature, but different acid concentrations
Different metals, different acid volumes, and different temperatures
Same acid concentration, but one tube has a catalyst and one has no metal
Different acids, different masses, and no timing
questions.correctAnswer: Same magnesium length and temperature, but different acid concentrations
questions.explanation: A fair comparison changes concentration only while keeping other variables constant and measuring the reaction time or gas produced.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse experimental design for reaction rate investigations.

questions.prompt: For a reaction involving gases, why can increasing pressure increase the rate?
options: Gas particles are closer together, so collisions are more frequent
Gas particles disappear from the container
Pressure changes gases into solids instantly
All gas particles stop moving
questions.correctAnswer: Gas particles are closer together, so collisions are more frequent
questions.explanation: Increasing pressure compresses gas particles into a smaller volume, increasing the chance of successful collisions.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse the effect of pressure on reaction rates involving gases.

questions.prompt: What is the moment of a force about a pivot?
options: Force multiplied by perpendicular distance from the pivot
Mass divided by temperature
Distance multiplied by time
Pressure divided by volume
questions.correctAnswer: Force multiplied by perpendicular distance from the pivot
questions.explanation: The turning effect of a force depends on the size of the force and its perpendicular distance from the pivot.
questions.learningOutcome: State the meaning of moment of a force.

questions.prompt: What is the SI unit of the moment of a force?
options: Newton metre
Newton per metre
Metre per second
Kilogram per cubic metre
questions.correctAnswer: Newton metre
questions.explanation: Moment is calculated as force in newtons multiplied by distance in metres, giving newton metre.
questions.learningOutcome: Identify the unit used for moment of a force.

questions.prompt: A 10 N force acts 0.30 m from a pivot at right angles. What is the moment about the pivot?
options: 3.0 N m
30 N m
questions.correctAnswer: 3.0 N m
questions.explanation: Moment equals force times perpendicular distance: 10 N x 0.30 m = 3.0 N m.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate moment of a force using force and perpendicular distance.

questions.prompt: A balanced see-saw has a 300 N learner 2 m from the pivot on one side. Where should a 600 N learner sit on the other side?
options: 1 m from the pivot
2 m from the pivot
3 m from the pivot
4 m from the pivot
questions.correctAnswer: 1 m from the pivot
questions.explanation: For balance, clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal. 300 x 2 = 600 N m, so 600 N needs 1 m.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply the principle of moments to a balanced system.

questions.prompt: Why does a longer spanner make it easier to loosen a tight nut?
options: It increases the perpendicular distance from the pivot, increasing the moment
It reduces the force of gravity to zero
It changes the nut into a magnet
It removes friction from the threads completely
questions.correctAnswer: It increases the perpendicular distance from the pivot, increasing the moment
questions.explanation: For the same applied force, a longer distance from the pivot produces a larger turning effect.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply moments to everyday tools and machines.

questions.prompt: Two equal and opposite parallel forces act at different points on a steering wheel. What do they form?
options: A couple that produces rotation
A single upward force only
A chemical bond
A stationary electric charge
questions.correctAnswer: A couple that produces rotation
questions.explanation: A couple consists of two equal, opposite, parallel forces whose lines of action are separated, producing a turning effect.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse turning effects produced by anti-parallel forces.

questions.prompt: A door is hardest to open when pushed near the hinges. Which analysis best explains this?
options: The perpendicular distance from the pivot is small, so the moment is small
The door has no mass near the hinges
The force changes into heat before reaching the door
The hinges remove the need for any turning effect
questions.correctAnswer: The perpendicular distance from the pivot is small, so the moment is small
questions.explanation: Pushing near the hinge gives a small lever arm, so a larger force is needed to produce the same turning effect.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse how distance from pivot affects practical turning effects.

questions.prompt: What is acceleration?
options: Rate of change of velocity
Total distance travelled
Mass per unit volume
Force multiplied by distance from a pivot
questions.correctAnswer: Rate of change of velocity
questions.explanation: Acceleration describes how quickly velocity changes with time.
questions.learningOutcome: Define acceleration in linear motion.

questions.prompt: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
options: Speed
Mass
Temperature
Pressure
questions.correctAnswer: Speed
questions.explanation: The gradient of a distance-time graph is change in distance divided by change in time, which gives speed.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret distance-time graphs for motion.

questions.prompt: On a velocity-time graph, what does the area under the graph represent?
options: Displacement
Density
Moment
Electric current
questions.correctAnswer: Displacement
questions.explanation: Multiplying velocity by time gives displacement, so the area under a velocity-time graph represents displacement.
questions.learningOutcome: Interpret velocity-time graphs for linear motion.

questions.prompt: A cyclist increases velocity from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 s. What is the acceleration?
options: 2 m/s2
3 m/s2
questions.correctAnswer: 2 m/s2
questions.explanation: Acceleration equals change in velocity divided by time: (16 - 4) / 6 = 2 m/s2.
questions.learningOutcome: Calculate acceleration from change in velocity and time.

questions.prompt: Ignoring air resistance, why does a dropped stone speed up as it falls near Earth's surface?
options: Gravity gives it an approximately constant downward acceleration
The stone becomes lighter every second
Air pushes the stone upward faster
The stone produces its own engine force
questions.correctAnswer: Gravity gives it an approximately constant downward acceleration
questions.explanation: Near Earth's surface, gravity accelerates falling objects downward at about 9.8 m/s2 when air resistance is ignored.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply constant acceleration ideas to falling bodies.

questions.prompt: A velocity-time graph is a straight line sloping upward from the origin. Which motion does it show?
options: Uniform acceleration from rest
Uniform speed with no acceleration
Object at rest for the whole time
Random motion with no pattern
questions.correctAnswer: Uniform acceleration from rest
questions.explanation: A straight rising velocity-time graph has constant gradient, so acceleration is constant. Starting at the origin means initial velocity is zero.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse velocity-time graphs for constant acceleration.

questions.prompt: In wave motion, what is amplitude?
options: Maximum displacement from the rest position
Number of waves produced per second
Distance travelled by light in a year
Time taken for one chemical reaction
questions.correctAnswer: Maximum displacement from the rest position
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the greatest displacement of a vibrating particle from its equilibrium position.
questions.learningOutcome: Define terms used in waves.

questions.prompt: What is frequency in wave motion?
options: Number of complete waves passing a point each second
Maximum height of one crest above the rest line
Distance between a crest and the next trough only
Amount of salt dissolved in water
questions.correctAnswer: Number of complete waves passing a point each second
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz and counts how many complete waves pass a point in one second.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain frequency as a wave quantity.

questions.prompt: A water wave has frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 2 m. What is its speed?
options: 10 m/s
7 m/s
questions.correctAnswer: 10 m/s
questions.explanation: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: 5 Hz x 2 m = 10 m/s.
questions.learningOutcome: Use the wave equation to calculate wave speed.

questions.prompt: Which example shows refraction rather than reflection?
options: A straw appears bent where it enters water
A plane mirror forms an image of a face
An echo returns from a cliff
A ball bounces from a wall
questions.correctAnswer: A straw appears bent where it enters water
questions.explanation: Refraction is bending of a wave when it changes speed moving between media, such as light passing from air into water.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply properties of waves to real-life observations.

questions.prompt: Water waves move from deep water into shallow water at an angle. What happens to the wave direction?
options: The waves slow down and bend toward the normal
The waves speed up and bend away from the normal
The waves stop carrying energy
The waves become chemical bonds
questions.correctAnswer: The waves slow down and bend toward the normal
questions.explanation: In shallow water, water waves travel more slowly. At an angle, this speed change causes refraction toward the normal.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse refraction of waves as speed changes between regions.

questions.prompt: A learner brings the north pole of one bar magnet close to the north pole of another. What happens?
options: The poles repel each other
The poles attract each other strongly
Both magnets lose all magnetism instantly
The poles produce electric current without motion
questions.correctAnswer: The poles repel each other
questions.explanation: Like magnetic poles repel, while unlike magnetic poles attract.
questions.learningOutcome: Apply the law of magnetic poles to predict attraction or repulsion.

questions.prompt: How are magnetic field lines drawn outside a bar magnet?
options: From the north pole to the south pole
From the south pole to the north pole only
In random circles that never meet poles
Only inside the wooden bench below the magnet
questions.correctAnswer: From the north pole to the south pole
questions.explanation: Outside a magnet, field lines are represented as leaving the north pole and entering the south pole.
questions.learningOutcome: Represent magnetic fields around a bar magnet.

questions.prompt: A coil connected to a sensitive galvanometer deflects only when a magnet is moved into or out of the coil. What causes the deflection?
options: A changing magnetic field induces an electromotive force in the coil
The stationary magnet heats the wire until it glows
The coil changes into a permanent magnet without current
The galvanometer detects sound waves from the magnet
questions.correctAnswer: A changing magnetic field induces an electromotive force in the coil
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic induction occurs when a changing magnetic field linked with a conductor produces an induced emf.
questions.learningOutcome: Explain electromagnetic induction using a magnet and coil.

questions.prompt: Which change would increase the induced emf in a simple coil and magnet experiment?
options: Move a stronger magnet faster through a coil with more turns
Keep the magnet still far from the coil
Remove all turns from the coil
Replace the coil with dry paper only
questions.correctAnswer: Move a stronger magnet faster through a coil with more turns
questions.explanation: A stronger field, faster change of field, and more coil turns all increase the induced emf.
questions.learningOutcome: Analyse factors affecting the magnitude of induced emf.

questions.prompt: Which classroom setup best demonstrates electromagnetic induction safely?
options: Move a bar magnet in and out of an insulated coil connected to a galvanometer
Connect a bare wire directly across a mains socket
Heat a magnet with a flame until it glows
Drop iron filings into acid and smell the gas
questions.correctAnswer: Move a bar magnet in and out of an insulated coil connected to a galvanometer
questions.explanation: A moving magnet and insulated coil connected to a galvanometer safely shows induced current without using dangerous mains electricity.
questions.learningOutcome: Select a safe practical setup for demonstrating electromagnetic induction.
